html:
Week 2 Overview

Why Phases A–E Are Critical

Week 1 gave you the 10,000-foot view of the ADM. Week 2 goes deep. The Level 1 exam tests ADM knowledge at two levels:

  1. Sequence — Which phase comes before/after which? What triggers what?
  2. Content — What are the formal inputs, steps, and outputs of each phase?

Phases A–E are where all architecture is designed. Phases F–H (Week 3) are where it is delivered and sustained. If you understand Phases A–E deeply, you have the foundation to answer the majority of exam questions.

Exam Weight Distribution for This Week's Content

Phase Approximate Exam Coverage
Phase A: Architecture Vision 8–10%
Phase B: Business Architecture 8–10%
Phase C: Information Systems (Data + Application) 10–12%
Phase D: Technology Architecture 6–8%
Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions 8–10%
Cross-phase concepts (ADD, roadmap, gap analysis) 5–8%
Total for Week 2 content ~45–55% of exam

Study Schedule

Day Topic Study Time
Monday Phase A: Architecture Vision 3 hours
Tuesday Phase B: Business Architecture 3 hours
Wednesday Phase C Part 1: Data Architecture 3 hours
Thursday Phase C Part 2: Application Architecture 3 hours
Friday Phase D: Technology Architecture 3 hours
Saturday Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions 3 hours
Sunday Cross-phase concepts + Quiz 3 hours

A Note on TOGAF's Formal Steps

Each ADM phase has formally defined steps in the TOGAF 9.2 specification. These steps follow the same general pattern:

Step 1: Select reference models, viewpoints, and tools
Step 2: Develop Baseline (AS-IS) description
Step 3: Develop Target (TO-BE) description
Step 4: Perform Gap Analysis
Step 5: Define candidate roadmap components
Step 6: Resolve impacts across the Architecture Landscape
Step 7: Conduct formal stakeholder review
Step 8: Finalize the architecture
Step 9: Create/update Architecture Definition Document

This pattern repeats for Phases B, C, and D. The exam tests whether you know this pattern and the phase-specific variations. Phase A and Phase E have different step structures because their purpose is different.

Day 1: Phase A — Architecture Vision

What Phase A Is

Phase A is the first phase after the Preliminary Phase. It is where a specific architecture initiative begins. If the Preliminary Phase sets up the framework (the rules of the game), Phase A starts a specific game (a specific architecture project).

Phase A answers: What problem are we solving, for whom, to what end, and with what boundaries?

Phase A does NOT produce a detailed architecture. It produces a high-level vision — enough to get sponsorship and approval to do the detailed work in Phases B, C, D.

Formal Objectives of Phase A

  1. Develop a high-level aspirational vision of the target capabilities and business value
  2. Obtain approval for a Statement of Architecture Work to proceed
  3. Identify the stakeholders and their concerns
  4. Confirm business goals, drivers, and constraints
  5. Define the scope of the architecture effort
  6. Develop and refine Architecture Principles (if not already established)
  7. Develop a Communications Plan

What Triggers Phase A?

Phase A is triggered by a Request for Architecture Work.

This is a formal document — not an email, not a verbal request. It is issued by the business or IT leadership sponsoring the architecture effort. It answers:

  • Why is this architecture work needed?
  • Who is sponsoring it?
  • What is the rough scope?
  • What are the business drivers?
Exam tip

"Request for Architecture Work" is the formal TOGAF name for the Phase A trigger. Exam questions use this exact phrase. A common distractor is "Architecture Brief" or "Project Charter" — these are wrong in TOGAF context.

The Formal Steps of Phase A (11 Steps)

Phase A's steps are different from the standard pattern (B, C, D) because it's about vision, not architecture design:

Step 1: Establish the Architecture Project

  • Confirm the business context and the architecture team
  • Identify the Architecture Sponsor (senior executive with authority and accountability)
  • Establish architecture team and assign roles

Step 2: Identify Stakeholders, Concerns, and Business Requirements

  • Create a Stakeholder Map — who has interests in the architecture?
  • Document stakeholder Concerns — what does each stakeholder care about?
  • Map concerns to architecture requirements
  • This is foundational: if you don't understand stakeholder concerns, you'll create views nobody needs

Step 3: Confirm and Elaborate Business Goals, Drivers, and Constraints

  • Business goals: what the organization wants to achieve
  • Business drivers: why change is needed now (market pressure, regulation, opportunity)
  • Constraints: what limits the architecture (budget, regulation, existing systems, timelines)
  • Both goals AND constraints must be documented — constraints are as important as goals

Step 4: Evaluate Business Capabilities

  • Assess the current capability of the organization to execute the architecture work
  • Identify capability gaps that will affect the architecture program itself

Step 5: Assess Readiness for Business Transformation

  • How ready is the organization to change?
  • Cultural, process, and technical change capacity
  • This affects how ambitious the target architecture can be and how fast transition can happen

Step 6: Define Scope

  • What is IN scope vs. OUT of scope?
  • Which business units, geographies, systems are included?
  • What is the level of detail needed?
  • Scope defined here controls the entire ADM cycle — scope creep in Phase A means rework in Phases B–H

Step 7: Confirm and Elaborate Architecture Principles

  • Architecture Principles are the governing rules established in the Preliminary Phase
  • Phase A confirms these principles still apply to this initiative
  • May add initiative-specific principles
  • Examples: "Data is an Asset", "Technology Independence", "Single Source of Truth"
  • Principles have 4 parts: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications

Step 8: Develop Architecture Vision

  • The Architecture Vision document describes the target state at a high level
  • What capabilities will the organization have when done?
  • What business value will be delivered?
  • This is NOT a detailed architecture — it's a story of the future state
  • Technique used: Business Scenarios (see below)

Step 9: Define Target Architecture Value Propositions and KPIs

  • What measurable business outcomes will the architecture enable?
  • How will success be measured?
  • KPIs connect architecture to business value — critical for getting and maintaining sponsorship

Step 10: Identify Business Transformation Risks and Mitigation Activities

  • What could go wrong with this architecture initiative?
  • Risk categories: technology risk, business risk, organizational risk, regulatory risk
  • Document risks at this high level — detailed risk management happens throughout the ADM

Step 11: Develop Statement of Architecture Work; Secure Approval

  • The Statement of Architecture Work is the formal charter/agreement for the architecture project
  • It defines: scope, schedule, resources, deliverables, constraints, governance
  • Must be approved by the Architecture Sponsor before Phase B begins
  • This approval is a formal governance checkpoint — Phase B cannot start without it
Exam tip

Knowing ALL 11 steps is not as important as knowing the key ones: Step 2 (Stakeholder identification), Step 6 (Scope definition), Step 8 (Architecture Vision development), and Step 11 (Statement of Architecture Work approval). These are the most exam-tested.

Key Inputs to Phase A

Input Source Why It Matters
Request for Architecture Work Business/IT sponsor Triggers Phase A
Business Principles, Goals, Drivers Business strategy Defines what success looks like
Capability Assessment Organization Shows current capabilities and gaps
Tailored Architecture Framework Preliminary Phase Tells you how TOGAF has been customized
Organizational Model for EA Preliminary Phase Defines the EA team structure and governance
Architecture Repository Repository Existing models, standards, previous decisions

Key Outputs of Phase A

Output What It Is Exam Importance
Statement of Architecture Work Formal charter; scope, schedule, resources — signed by sponsor Very high — exam favorite
Architecture Vision High-level description of target capabilities and business value Very high
Communications Plan Who gets what information, when, and how Medium
Architecture Principles (refined) Governing rules, confirmed or updated High
Stakeholder Map and Concerns Who cares about what in the architecture High
Refined Business Goals, Drivers, Constraints Documented and agreed Medium
Architecture Vision Statement One-page summary of the vision Medium

Architecture Vision vs. Statement of Architecture Work

These are frequently confused. They are different documents with different purposes:

Architecture Vision Statement of Architecture Work
Answers What are we building? How are we going to build it?
Audience Business stakeholders, executives Architecture team, sponsors, governance
Content Target state description, business value, KPIs Scope, schedule, resources, deliverables, constraints
Analogy Project brief / concept Project charter
Used for Getting buy-in and understanding Formalizing the agreement

Both are outputs of Phase A. The Statement of Architecture Work must be approved before Phase B starts.

The Business Scenarios Technique

Business Scenarios is the primary technique TOGAF recommends for developing the Architecture Vision in Phase A.

What it is: A structured technique for identifying and describing the business problems the architecture must solve, from the perspective of the people affected.

A Business Scenario includes:

  1. A problem description (what's going wrong, or what opportunity exists)
  2. The business and technical environment
  3. The actors (human and technical) involved
  4. The desired outcomes (what "good" looks like)
  5. The human roles involved
  6. The computer roles involved

Why it matters for the exam: Business Scenarios is explicitly recommended by TOGAF for Phase A. If an exam question asks "What technique is used to develop the Architecture Vision?", the answer is Business Scenarios.

Scope Definition — Critical Concept

Scope in Phase A has 4 dimensions. All 4 must be defined:

Dimension Question Example
Breadth What business units/functions? HR and Finance only? Or the whole organization?
Depth How much detail is needed? High-level capability map? Or detailed process diagrams?
Time period Over what timeframe? 3-year target? Or 1-year target?
Domains Which architecture domains? All 4? Or only Technology?
Exam tip

TOGAF defines scope as having these 4 dimensions. Questions sometimes test which dimension is which. Breadth = width across the organization; Depth = level of detail.

Key Takeaway for Day 1 (Phase A)

Phase A is about defining the problem and getting formal approval to solve it. The two most important outputs are the Architecture Vision (what we're building) and the Statement of Architecture Work (the formal charter to build it). Phase B cannot start without signed approval of the Statement of Architecture Work.

Day 2: Phase B — Business Architecture

What Phase B Is

Phase B designs the Business Architecture — the first and most important of the four architecture domains.

Phase B answers: How is the business currently organized and how should it operate to achieve the target state defined in Phase A?

Business Architecture is designed FIRST because it drives all other domains. You cannot design the data architecture until you know what the business needs. You cannot design applications until you know what business processes they must support. You cannot design technology infrastructure until you know what applications will run on it.

The sequence is fixed for a reason:

Business (Phase B) → Data + Applications (Phase C) → Technology (Phase D)

Formal Objectives of Phase B

  1. Develop the Baseline Business Architecture (AS-IS — how the business works today)
  2. Develop the Target Business Architecture (TO-BE — how the business should work)
  3. Identify gaps between AS-IS and TO-BE
  4. Define candidate roadmap components (what work needs to be done to bridge the gap)
  5. Select and confirm Architecture Principles relevant to business
  6. Validate Phase A's Architecture Vision against business reality

The Formal Steps of Phase B (9 Steps)

Step 1: Select Reference Models, Viewpoints, and Tools

  • Choose which architecture viewpoints are relevant for the stakeholders
  • Identify reference models (e.g., industry-standard business models) that can be reused
  • Select modeling tools and notations (BPMN, ArchiMate, UML, etc.)

Step 2: Develop Baseline Business Architecture Description (AS-IS)

  • Document how the business currently works
  • Use existing documentation, interviews, process mining
  • Artifacts: organizational charts, current process flows, capability maps
  • This baseline is the "from" state — the starting point

Step 3: Develop Target Business Architecture Description (TO-BE)

  • Design how the business SHOULD work to achieve the vision from Phase A
  • This is the creative, strategic work
  • Artifacts: future-state organizational structure, redesigned processes, new capabilities
  • Constrained by: Phase A principles, scope, and constraints

Step 4: Perform Gap Analysis

  • Compare AS-IS to TO-BE systematically
  • Identify: What needs to be added? Changed? Removed? Retained as-is?
  • Output: Gap Analysis Results — the list of changes needed to get from current to target state
  • This directly feeds the roadmap

Step 5: Define Candidate Roadmap Components

  • Turn the Gap Analysis results into potential work items
  • These are high-level — detailed planning comes later in Phase F
  • At this stage: "We need to restructure the sales organization" not "We need to hire 5 people in Riyadh"

Step 6: Resolve Impacts Across the Architecture Landscape

  • Does this Business Architecture affect other architecture work in progress?
  • Example: If another team is redesigning the HR process, your Business Architecture changes may conflict
  • This step ensures integration across parallel architecture efforts

Step 7: Conduct Formal Stakeholder Review

  • Present the Business Architecture to relevant stakeholders for feedback
  • This is a formal governance checkpoint — not just an informal review
  • Stakeholders approve that the architecture correctly reflects their needs

Step 8: Finalize the Business Architecture

  • Incorporate feedback from stakeholder review
  • Sign off on the final Business Architecture
  • Baseline and Target are now formally accepted

Step 9: Create Architecture Definition Document (Business Architecture sections)

  • The ADD is built progressively — Phase B creates the Business Architecture sections
  • Phase C will add Data and Application sections; Phase D will add Technology sections
  • By end of Phase D, the ADD is complete across all 4 domains

Key Inputs to Phase B

Input Source
Architecture Vision (from Phase A) Phase A output
Statement of Architecture Work Phase A output — defines scope and constraints
Architecture Principles (especially Business Principles) Preliminary Phase / Phase A
Enterprise Continuum Architecture Repository — existing reference models
Existing business process documentation Organization
Organizational structure Business management

Key Outputs of Phase B

Output Description
Baseline Business Architecture AS-IS: how business works today
Target Business Architecture TO-BE: how business should work
Business Architecture components of ADD Documented architecture — both AS-IS and TO-BE
Business Architecture components of Architecture Requirements Specification Measurable business requirements
Business Architecture components of Architecture Roadmap Candidate work items from gap analysis
Updated Architecture Vision Refined based on business architecture insights

Business Capabilities vs. Business Processes — Key Distinction

This distinction is frequently tested and often confused:

Business Capability Business Process
Definition The ABILITY of the organization to do something HOW the organization does something
Example "Customer Relationship Management capability" "Customer onboarding process"
Question it answers What CAN we do? How DO we do it?
Stability Relatively stable (capabilities don't change often) Changes frequently as processes improve
Granularity Higher level More detailed
Artifact Business Capability Map Business Process Model (BPMN)
Driven by Business strategy Business operations
Exam tip

"Capability" is WHAT. "Process" is HOW. A capability can be supported by multiple processes. The Business Architecture covers both, but they are conceptually distinct.

Example:

  • Capability: "Order Fulfillment" (the ability to take and fulfill customer orders)
  • Process: "Receive order → Verify inventory → Pick items → Pack → Ship → Confirm delivery"
  • A capability exists even if the process changes. Capability maps are more stable than process maps.

Key Artifacts of Business Architecture

Artifact What It Shows Exam Relevance
Business Capability Map All organizational capabilities in a hierarchy High — often asked as an example artifact
Value Chain Diagram Sequential activities that create value (Porter's Value Chain) High — classic technique
Business Process Models (BPMN) Step-by-step process flows with swim lanes Medium
Organizational Map Who reports to whom; business units and relationships Medium
Business Interaction Matrix Which business units interact with which Medium
Actor/Role Matrix Which actors perform which roles in which processes Medium
Business Goals/Drivers Catalogue Documented goals and their drivers Medium

Gap Analysis in Phase B — How It Works

Gap Analysis is the technique of comparing the Baseline (AS-IS) to the Target (TO-BE) architecture.

AS-IS Business Architecture
     │
     │ ← Gap Analysis: What needs to change?
     │
     ▼
TO-BE Business Architecture

Gap Analysis Results — four outcomes (canonical TOGAF terms; common synonyms in brackets):
├── Added:      New capabilities/processes needed (don't exist today)
├── Changed:    Existing capabilities/processes that need modification [a.k.a. Improve/Enhance]
├── Eliminated: Capabilities/processes to be removed [a.k.a. Retire]
└── Retained:   What stays the same (no change needed)

Each item in the Gap Analysis becomes a candidate roadmap component — a potential piece of work in the Architecture Roadmap.

Exam tip

Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, and D — once per domain. The results from each phase are consolidated in Phase E to create the complete Architecture Roadmap.

Value Chain Analysis

Michael Porter's Value Chain is a classic Business Architecture technique TOGAF references:

Support Activities:
├── Firm Infrastructure
├── Human Resource Management
├── Technology Development
└── Procurement

Primary Activities (left to right, creating value):
Inbound Logistics → Operations → Outbound Logistics → Marketing & Sales → Service
                                                                              ↓
                                                                         MARGIN

In TOGAF context: A value chain diagram shows the primary and support activities that create value for the customer. Used to understand how the business creates value and where changes will have impact.

Key Takeaway for Day 2 (Phase B)

Business Architecture is the foundation for everything else. It must be done first (Phase B), before data, applications, or technology. Gap Analysis in Phase B produces candidate roadmap components. The Architecture Definition Document begins being built here — each subsequent phase adds to it.

Day 3: Phase C Part 1 — Data Architecture

What Data Architecture Is

Data Architecture is the first sub-phase of Phase C (Information Systems Architecture). It defines:

  • What data entities the organization has
  • How data is structured and related
  • How data flows through the organization
  • How data is governed and controlled
  • What data is needed (AS-IS) and what will be needed (TO-BE)

Data Architecture is designed BEFORE Application Architecture within Phase C. The reason is logical: you cannot correctly design the applications if you don't yet know what data they need to store, process, and share.

Formal Objectives of Data Architecture

  1. Define the types and sources of data needed to support the business (from Phase B)
  2. Create an enterprise data model (logical and physical)
  3. Understand data flows and data ownership
  4. Identify data governance requirements
  5. Perform Gap Analysis between current and target data landscape
  6. Define candidate roadmap components for data

The Formal Steps of Data Architecture (9 Steps — Same Pattern as Phase B)

Step 1: Select Reference Models, Viewpoints, and Tools

  • Choose relevant data architecture viewpoints (e.g., data owner viewpoint, regulatory viewpoint)
  • Reference models: industry data models (banking reference model, retail reference model, etc.)
  • Tools: ERD tools, data catalog tools, data flow diagram tools

Step 2: Develop Baseline Data Architecture Description (AS-IS)

  • Catalog all existing data entities and their sources
  • Document current data flows between systems
  • Identify data quality issues, silos, and redundancy
  • Artifact: Existing data model, data catalog, data flow diagrams

Step 3: Develop Target Data Architecture Description (TO-BE)

  • Design the target data landscape to support the Target Business Architecture from Phase B
  • What data entities need to exist? What are the relationships?
  • How should data flow? Where should master data reside?
  • Artifact: Target data model, target data flow diagrams

Step 4: Perform Gap Analysis

  • What data entities need to be created?
  • What existing data models need to change?
  • What data flows need to be created, modified, or retired?
  • What data governance policies are missing?
  • Output: Data Architecture Gap Analysis Results

Step 5: Define Candidate Roadmap Components

  • Each gap becomes a potential work item
  • Examples: "Implement Master Data Management for Customer entity", "Migrate product catalog to canonical data model"

Step 6: Resolve Impacts Across Architecture Landscape

  • Does this data architecture conflict with other data architecture work in progress?
  • How does it affect other segments of the enterprise?

Step 7: Conduct Formal Stakeholder Review

  • Data owners, data governance officers, privacy/compliance stakeholders
  • Formal sign-off required

Step 8: Finalize Data Architecture

  • Incorporate review feedback
  • Formal acceptance of AS-IS and TO-BE data architectures

Step 9: Create Architecture Definition Document (Data Architecture Sections)

  • Add Data Architecture sections to the ADD

Key Inputs to Data Architecture

Input Source
Business Architecture (from Phase B) Phase B output — defines what data the business needs
Existing data models and schemas Current systems documentation
Data governance policies Organization
Data standards Organization / industry
Architecture Repository Previous data architecture decisions

Key Outputs of Data Architecture

Output Description
Baseline Data Architecture AS-IS: current data entities, relationships, flows
Target Data Architecture TO-BE: future data landscape
Data Architecture components of ADD Documented in Architecture Definition Document
Data Architecture components of Architecture Requirements Specification Measurable data requirements (quality, latency, volume, etc.)
Data Architecture roadmap components Candidate work items

Core Concepts: Logical vs. Physical Data Models

Logical Data Model Physical Data Model
What Business entities and relationships, technology-independent Specific tables, columns, indexes, constraints for a specific database
Language Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERD), natural language SQL, database-specific notation
Audience Business analysts, data architects, business stakeholders Database administrators, developers
When created Target architecture design (Phase C) Implementation (later, project-level)
Example "Customer has many Orders" (ERD) CREATE TABLE customer (id INT, name VARCHAR(100)...)
Exam tip

TOGAF Data Architecture produces the logical data model. The physical model is implementation-specific and is usually created at project level, not enterprise architecture level. If a question asks what Phase C produces, the answer is the logical (not physical) model.

Key Data Architecture Artifacts

Artifact What It Shows Exam Relevance
Entity/Data Model Data entities, attributes, and relationships High
Data Flow Diagram (DFD) How data moves between processes and systems High
Conceptual/Logical Data Model Business-level view of data structure High
Data Migration Model How data will be moved from old to new systems Medium
Data Entity/Business Function Matrix Which business functions use which data entities High
Data Lifecycle Diagram How data is created, used, archived, and destroyed Medium
Data Security Diagram Who can access what data and under what conditions Medium

Master Data Management (MDM) — Important Concept

MDM is a data architecture concept heavily referenced in TOGAF contexts:

Master Data = the core shared data entities that are used across multiple systems (customers, products, employees, locations, suppliers, etc.)

The Problem: Without MDM, every system has its own version of "customer" — different formats, different IDs, different attributes — creating inconsistency, duplication, and quality problems.

The MDM Solution: A single "golden record" for each master data entity that all systems reference.

In TOGAF context: MDM decisions are made in the Data Architecture (Phase C). The target data architecture defines which entity is the master data source for each entity type.

Data Governance Connection

Data Architecture and Data Governance are closely linked:

  • Who owns the data? (Data Owner)
  • Who is responsible for data quality? (Data Steward)
  • What are the privacy and retention rules? (Data Policy)
  • How is access controlled? (Data Security Architecture)

Your CDMP background is a direct advantage here — you already understand data governance concepts. In TOGAF's data architecture, governance requirements from Phase B (business rules about data) must be reflected in the data model and data flows.

Key Takeaway for Day 3 (Data Architecture)

Data Architecture (Phase C, first sub-phase) defines the logical data landscape — entities, relationships, and flows. It produces the logical data model, data flow diagrams, and gap analysis. It must be completed before Application Architecture because applications depend on what data exists and how it is structured.

Day 4: Phase C Part 2 — Application Architecture

What Application Architecture Is

Application Architecture is the second sub-phase of Phase C. It defines:

  • What application systems the organization has and needs
  • How applications interact and communicate
  • Which applications support which business processes
  • What interfaces exist between applications
  • What applications will be retired, replaced, or created

Application Architecture is designed AFTER Data Architecture because:

  • Applications need to know what data they will store and process
  • Interface design depends on what data flows between applications
  • Application portfolio decisions are influenced by the data architecture

Formal Objectives of Application Architecture

  1. Define the application systems needed to support the Business Architecture (Phase B) and Data Architecture (Phase C Part 1)
  2. Create an Application Portfolio showing all current and planned applications
  3. Define Application Interfaces — how applications communicate
  4. Identify redundant applications that can be rationalized or decommissioned
  5. Perform Gap Analysis between current and target application landscape
  6. Define candidate roadmap components

The Formal Steps of Application Architecture (9 Steps — Same Pattern)

Step 1: Select Reference Models, Viewpoints, and Tools

  • Application architecture viewpoints (portfolio view, interface view, etc.)
  • Reference: TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM), industry application models
  • Tools: ArchiMate, UML, Enterprise Architect modeling tools

Step 2: Develop Baseline Application Architecture Description (AS-IS)

  • Catalog all existing applications
  • Document what each application does and what data it owns or consumes
  • Document current interfaces between applications
  • Identify technical debt: aging, redundant, or unsupported applications
  • Artifact: Current Application Portfolio Map

Step 3: Develop Target Application Architecture Description (TO-BE)

  • Which applications will exist in the target state?
  • What new applications are needed to support new business capabilities?
  • Which existing applications will be:
    • Retained — kept as-is
    • Improved — enhanced
    • Replaced — new system replaces old
    • Retired — decommissioned
  • How will applications interface in the target state?
  • Artifact: Target Application Portfolio Map, Target Interface Catalog

Step 4: Perform Gap Analysis

  • What applications need to be created?
  • What applications need to be modified?
  • What applications need to be retired?
  • What new interfaces need to be built?
  • Output: Application Architecture Gap Analysis Results

Step 5: Define Candidate Roadmap Components

  • Each gap becomes a potential work item
  • Examples: "Implement CRM system", "Retire legacy billing system", "Build API gateway"

Steps 6–9: Same pattern as Data Architecture (resolve impacts, stakeholder review, finalize, add to ADD)

Key Inputs to Application Architecture

Input Source
Business Architecture (Phase B) Defines what processes applications must support
Data Architecture (Phase C Part 1) Defines what data applications must store/process
Existing application inventory Organization
Integration standards Organization / industry
Enterprise Continuum Reference application architectures

Key Outputs of Application Architecture

Output Description
Baseline Application Architecture AS-IS: current application landscape
Target Application Architecture TO-BE: future application landscape
Application Architecture components of ADD Documented in Architecture Definition Document
Application Architecture components of Architecture Requirements Specification Measurable app requirements (availability, performance, scalability)
Application Architecture roadmap components Candidate work items

Key Application Architecture Artifacts

Artifact What It Shows Exam Relevance
Application Portfolio Map All applications, their status and relationships Very High
Application Communication Diagram How applications communicate/integrate Very High
Application Interface Catalog All interfaces with details (protocol, frequency, data) High
Application/Business Function Matrix Which application supports which business function High
Application/Organization Matrix Which business units use which applications Medium
Application Interaction Matrix Applications and their interactions (matrix view) Medium
Application Migration Diagram Transition from current to future application landscape Medium

Application Portfolio Rationalization

A key activity in Application Architecture is rationalization: reducing application sprawl.

Common patterns found in AS-IS analysis:

  • Duplication: Multiple applications doing the same thing (e.g., 3 different spreadsheet tools for reporting)
  • Shadow IT: Unofficial applications built by business units outside IT governance
  • Legacy systems: Old applications on unsupported technology (often the hardest to retire)
  • Over-customized COTS: Commercial-off-the-shelf software so customized it can't be upgraded

Target state decisions for each application (the TIME model):

For each application, decide:
├── Tolerate  — Keep as-is for now; low value but adequate technical health (watch for retirement)
├── Invest    — Keep and enhance; high value, good technical health (strategic)
├── Migrate   — Replace / re-platform; high value but poor technical health
└── Eliminate — Decommission; low value, no longer worth keeping (a.k.a. Retire)

This four-category framework is the TIME model (Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, Eliminate) — the standard application-portfolio rationalization framework, covered in detail in Week 5. It is commonly referenced in exam contexts.

Application Interfaces — Critical Concept

Interface design is central to Application Architecture. Key interface concepts:

Synchronous vs. Asynchronous:

  • Synchronous — Caller waits for response (REST API call, database query)
  • Asynchronous — Caller sends and doesn't wait (message queue, event stream)

Point-to-point vs. Integration platform:

  • Point-to-point — Each system connects directly to every other (messy, hard to maintain)
  • Integration platform — All systems connect through a hub (ESB, API gateway, message broker)

In TOGAF context: the Application Interface Catalog documents all interfaces, their protocols, frequency, and direction of data flow. This connects to the Data Architecture (what data flows) and Technology Architecture (what platform carries the data).

Exam tip

Phase C produces the Application Interface Catalog. This is distinct from the Technology Architecture (Phase D), which defines the technology that carries the interfaces (e.g., Kafka, REST, SOAP). Application Architecture says "there is an interface here"; Technology Architecture says "it runs on this platform".

Key Takeaway for Day 4 (Application Architecture)

Application Architecture (Phase C, second sub-phase) defines what applications exist, what they do, and how they talk to each other. It produces the Application Portfolio Map and Interface Catalog. Application Architecture is designed AFTER Data Architecture because applications depend on the data model. It feeds directly into Technology Architecture, which defines the platform that runs the applications.

Day 5: Phase D — Technology Architecture

What Phase D Is

Phase D designs the Technology Architecture — the infrastructure layer that everything runs on. It is the last architecture design phase before the transition to implementation planning (Phase E).

Phase D answers: What technology platforms, standards, and infrastructure are needed to run the applications and data defined in Phase C?

Technology Architecture is designed LAST of the four domains because:

  • Technology must support the applications (Phase C Application Architecture)
  • Technology choices are constrained by data requirements (Phase C Data Architecture)
  • Technology decisions must enable the business capabilities (Phase B)
  • Only after all three of the above are designed can you make correct technology choices

Formal Objectives of Phase D

  1. Develop the Baseline Technology Architecture (AS-IS — current technology landscape)
  2. Develop the Target Technology Architecture (TO-BE — future technology landscape)
  3. Identify the technology components needed to support the application and data architectures
  4. Define Technology Standards — what platforms and technologies the organization will use
  5. Create a Technology Roadmap — the plan for evolving the technology landscape
  6. Perform Gap Analysis
  7. Define candidate roadmap components

The Formal Steps of Phase D (9 Steps — Same Pattern as B and C)

Step 1: Select Reference Models, Viewpoints, and Tools

  • TOGAF's Technical Reference Model (TRM) is the primary reference model for Phase D
  • The TRM provides a standard taxonomy of technology components (see below)
  • Technology standards repositories inform standards selection

Step 2: Develop Baseline Technology Architecture Description (AS-IS)

  • Catalog current hardware, software platforms, operating systems, middleware, networks
  • Identify technical debt: aging infrastructure, unsupported platforms, end-of-life systems
  • Document current technology standards (or their absence)
  • Artifact: Current Infrastructure Diagrams, Current Technology Standards Matrix

Step 3: Develop Target Technology Architecture Description (TO-BE)

  • What technology platform is needed to run the target applications (from Phase C)?
  • What technology standards should the organization adopt?
  • Cloud vs. on-premise vs. hybrid decisions
  • Platform selection: which database? which middleware? which cloud provider?
  • Artifact: Target Infrastructure Diagrams, Target Technology Standards

Step 4: Perform Gap Analysis

  • What technology components need to be acquired or built?
  • What existing technology needs to be upgraded or replaced?
  • What technology needs to be retired?
  • Output: Technology Architecture Gap Analysis Results

Step 5: Define Candidate Roadmap Components

  • Each technology gap becomes a work item
  • Examples: "Migrate from on-premise to Azure", "Upgrade database from SQL Server 2012 to SQL Server 2022", "Implement API gateway"

Steps 6–9: Same pattern (resolve impacts, stakeholder review, finalize, add to ADD)

Key Inputs to Phase D

Input Source
Information Systems Architecture (Phase C) Applications and data architecture from Phase C
Architecture Vision (Phase A) High-level constraints and vision
Existing technology standards Organization
Infrastructure capacity data IT operations
Technology vendor roadmaps Vendors — when is this product EOL?
TOGAF TRM TOGAF reference model for technology taxonomy

Key Outputs of Phase D

Output Description
Baseline Technology Architecture AS-IS: current infrastructure
Target Technology Architecture TO-BE: future technology landscape
Technology Architecture components of ADD Added to the Architecture Definition Document
Technology Architecture components of Architecture Requirements Specification Performance, availability, scalability requirements
Technology Architecture roadmap components Candidate work items
Technology Reference Architecture The organization's specific technology reference model
Technology Standards Matrix What technologies are approved, and for what use

TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM)

The TRM is TOGAF's reference model for technology (Part VI of TOGAF 9.2). It provides a standard taxonomy and terminology for technology components.

The TRM has two main components:

1. The TRM Taxonomy: A classification of all technology services into categories:

TRM Taxonomy:
├── Infrastructure Applications
│   ├── Collaboration Services (email, messaging, conferencing)
│   ├── Operations and Management Services
│   └── Repository Services
├── Application Platform
│   ├── Data Management Services (databases)
│   ├── Transaction Processing Services
│   ├── Presentation Services (UI)
│   ├── Network Services
│   └── Integration Services (middleware, APIs)
└── Communications Infrastructure
    ├── Network Services
    └── Hardware

2. The TRM Diagram: A visual representation showing layers of technology from infrastructure up to applications.

Exam tip

Know that TRM is the TOGAF reference model for Technology Architecture and that it provides a taxonomy of technology services. You don't need to memorize every category, but you should know what the TRM is and what it is used for. Common exam question: "What TOGAF reference model is used in Phase D?" → TRM.

Technology Standards Matrix

The Technology Standards Matrix is a key artifact of Phase D:

Technology Category Current Standard Target Standard Status
Relational Database Oracle 11g PostgreSQL 14 Migrate
Application Server WebLogic 12 Spring Boot / Docker Migrate
Message Broker IBM MQ Apache Kafka Migrate
Cloud Platform On-premise Microsoft Azure Migrate
API Gateway None Azure API Management Add

This matrix communicates:

  • What technology is used today (AS-IS)
  • What technology should be used (TO-BE)
  • What action is needed (retain, migrate, add, retire)

Technology Architecture Viewpoints

Different stakeholders need different views of the technology architecture:

Stakeholder Viewpoint What They Need to See
CIO Strategic technology view Technology roadmap, cost, risk
Infrastructure Manager Platform view Servers, storage, network topology
Security Officer Security view Firewalls, zones, encryption, access control
Operations Team Deployment view How applications are deployed on infrastructure
Developer Development platform view Development tools, environments, CI/CD pipeline
Exam tip

Creating viewpoints tailored to stakeholder concerns is a core TOGAF concept. Phase D should produce technology views relevant to the stakeholders identified in Phase A. This connects Phase A (Stakeholder Map) to Phase D (creating Views for each Viewpoint).

Technology Lifecycle Decisions

Phase D must consider the lifecycle of every technology component:

  • Invest — Strategic technology; increase investment
  • Migrate — Plan to replace this technology within the roadmap period
  • Tolerate — Keep for now, but watch; don't invest further
  • Retire/Eliminate — Decommission; plan the exit

This mirrors the application portfolio rationalization in Phase C. Together, they drive the implementation roadmap in Phase E.

Key Takeaway for Day 5 (Phase D)

Technology Architecture (Phase D) defines the infrastructure, platforms, and standards needed to run the applications and data from Phase C. It uses the TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM) as a reference. It produces the Technology Standards Matrix and feeds candidate roadmap components into Phase E. After Phase D, all four architecture domains have been designed and the ADD is complete.

Day 6: Phase E — Opportunities & Solutions

What Phase E Is

Phase E is the bridge between architecture design and implementation planning. It is the first phase where the focus shifts from designing the architecture to planning how to deliver it.

By the end of Phase D, you have:

  • A complete Baseline Architecture (AS-IS) covering all 4 domains
  • A complete Target Architecture (TO-BE) covering all 4 domains
  • Gap Analysis results from Phases B, C, and D (three separate gap analyses)
  • Candidate roadmap components from Phases B, C, and D (fragmented, not yet integrated)

Phase E takes all of this and:

  1. Consolidates the fragmented gap analysis results into a coherent picture
  2. Groups related gaps into Work Packages
  3. Sequences the work packages into a logical implementation order
  4. Defines Transition Architectures — the intermediate states between AS-IS and TO-BE
  5. Produces the first complete version of the Architecture Roadmap

The Critical Distinction: Phase E vs. Phase F

This is one of the most commonly confused distinctions on the exam:

Phase E Phase F
Focus WHAT work to do and in what rough sequence HOW to do it: detailed plan, resources, costs
Output Architecture Roadmap v0.1, Work Packages, Transition Architectures Detailed Implementation and Migration Plan, finalized roadmap
Level of detail Strategic, high-level Tactical, detailed
Question it answers What are the work packages and in what order? When exactly, by whom, at what cost?
Architecture Roadmap version Version 0.1 (initial) Finalized (complete)
Exam tip

If a question asks "Where is the Architecture Roadmap first produced in complete form?", the answer is Phase E (as Version 0.1). If it asks "Where is the Architecture Roadmap finalized?", the answer is Phase F.

Formal Objectives of Phase E

  1. Determine the overall Implementation Strategy (big bang, phased, parallel running, etc.)
  2. Consolidate and review Gap Analysis results from Phases B, C, and D
  3. Group gaps into Work Packages with related activities
  4. Define and prioritize Transition Architectures
  5. Create the Architecture Roadmap (Version 0.1)
  6. Initiate the Implementation and Migration Plan (Version 0.1)
  7. Assess business value vs. implementation risk for each work package

The Formal Steps of Phase E (11 Steps)

Phase E has more steps than B, C, and D because it's more complex — it integrates everything:

Step 1: Determine/Confirm Key Corporate Change Attributes

  • How does this organization handle change? Fast or incremental?
  • What is the organizational change capacity?
  • This shapes how ambitious the transition plan can be

Step 2: Determine Business Constraints for Implementation

  • Financial constraints: How much can be spent?
  • Resource constraints: What skills and people are available?
  • Regulatory constraints: What must be done first to remain compliant?
  • Technology constraints: What dependencies exist between work packages?

Step 3: Review and Consolidate Gap Analysis Results from Phases B to D

  • Take the three separate gap analyses (Business, Data/Application, Technology) and consolidate them
  • Cross-domain gaps become visible at this stage
  • Example: A business process change (Phase B gap) requires a new application (Phase C gap) which requires new infrastructure (Phase D gap) — these three gaps are actually one integrated work package

Step 4: Review Consolidated Requirements Across Related Business Functions

  • Ensure requirements from different business functions are reconciled
  • Conflicting requirements must be resolved before planning

Step 5: Consolidate and Reconcile Interoperability Requirements

  • Define what interoperability is needed between systems and architectures
  • Interoperability: the ability of different systems to work together

Step 6: Refine and Validate Dependencies

  • Which work packages depend on other work packages?
  • What is the critical path?
  • You cannot implement the application until the infrastructure is ready (technology dependency)
  • You cannot retire the old system until the new system is live (operational dependency)

Step 7: Confirm Readiness and Risk for Business Transformation

  • Updated assessment of organizational readiness
  • Are the risks acceptable given the current environment?
  • This may trigger scope adjustments

Step 8: Formulate Implementation and Migration Strategy

  • Choose the overall approach to moving from AS-IS to TO-BE:
    • Big Bang: Move everything at once (high risk, fast)
    • Incremental: Move in phases, domain by domain or function by function (lower risk, slower)
    • Parallel Running: Run old and new systems simultaneously during transition (safe but expensive)
    • Greenfield: Build the target state entirely new alongside the current state

Step 9: Identify and Group Major Work Packages

  • A Work Package is a bundle of related work items that can be scheduled and assigned
  • Criteria for grouping: technical dependency, business priority, risk, resource needs
  • Each work package has: scope, estimated effort, dependencies, business value, risk

Step 10: Identify Transition Architectures

  • The Transition Architecture is an intermediate, stable, deployable state between AS-IS and TO-BE
  • There may be 1, 2, 3, or more transition architectures depending on complexity
  • Each transition architecture is a coherent state the organization can operate in
  • Example:
    AS-IS (on-premise, monolith)
  → Transition Arch 1: Lift-and-shift to cloud (infrastructure moves, app unchanged)
  → Transition Arch 2: Application refactoring to microservices (still cloud)
  → TO-BE (cloud-native, microservices, event-driven)
  • Transition architectures enable phased delivery — you don't have to wait for everything to be done to get some value

Step 11: Create the Architecture Roadmap and Implementation and Migration Plan

  • Architecture Roadmap v0.1: Sequenced list of work packages with their transition architectures
  • Implementation and Migration Plan v0.1: Higher-level view of what will be built and when
  • These are version 0.1 — they will be finalized in Phase F

Key Inputs to Phase E

Input Source
Gap Analysis results from Phases B, C, D Outputs of Phases B, C, D
Architecture Definition Document (draft, all 4 domains) Built through Phases B, C, D
Architecture Principles Preliminary Phase / Phase A
Architecture Roadmap components (from Phases B, C, D) Candidate components, not yet integrated
Capability Assessment Phase A output
Resource availability and constraints Business management

Key Outputs of Phase E

Output Version Description
Architecture Roadmap Version 0.1 First integrated, complete roadmap across all domains
Implementation and Migration Plan Version 0.1 Initial plan showing what will be built
Work Package list — All identified work packages with scope, priority, dependency
Transition Architecture(s) — Defined intermediate stable states
Updated Architecture Definition Document — ADD refined based on Phase E insights
Updated Architecture Vision — Refined if scope changes occurred
Benefits Diagram — Shows how work packages map to business benefits

Work Packages — Detailed Definition

A Work Package is a unit of implementation that:

  • Has a clear scope (what is included and what is not)
  • Can be assigned to a project or team
  • Has a defined set of deliverables
  • Has dependencies on other work packages
  • Has an estimated effort and cost
  • Has a measurable business benefit

Work Package characteristics:

Work Package: "Implement Customer Master Data Management"
├── Scope: Customer data entity management across CRM, ERP, and e-commerce
├── Deliverables: MDM platform, customer golden record, integration to 3 systems
├── Dependencies: Requires "ERP Platform Upgrade" (WP-003) to be complete first
├── Estimated effort: 6 months, 4 architects + 8 developers
├── Business value: Eliminate duplicate customer records (estimated 12% customer data duplication)
└── Risk: High — requires significant data migration and parallel running

Architecture Roadmap — How It's Built

The Architecture Roadmap is built incrementally across Phases B through E:

Phase B → Business Architecture roadmap components
            (business process changes, capability additions)

Phase C → Data Architecture roadmap components
            (data migrations, MDM implementations, new data flows)
           Application Architecture roadmap components
            (new apps, retirements, interface buildouts)

Phase D → Technology Architecture roadmap components
            (infrastructure changes, platform migrations, standards adoption)

Phase E → FIRST COMPLETE ROADMAP (v0.1)
            All components integrated, sequenced, and organized into
            Work Packages with Transition Architectures

Transition Architectures — Why They Matter

Without Transition Architectures, the only options are:

  1. Big Bang (risky, painful, often fails)
  2. Never reaching the target state (paralysis)

With Transition Architectures:

  • Business gets value at each transition milestone
  • Risk is managed by delivering incrementally
  • Each transition state is stable enough to run operations on
  • If a later transition proves infeasible, the organization is still in a working state
Exam tip

Transition Architectures are defined in Phase E (not Phase F). Phase F uses them as the basis for the detailed migration plan. A question asking "where are Transition Architectures first defined?" → Phase E.

Key Takeaway for Day 6 (Phase E)

Phase E is the integration phase. It consolidates all three domain gap analyses, groups gaps into Work Packages, defines Transition Architectures, and produces the first complete Architecture Roadmap (v0.1). It is the bridge between architecture design (Phases B–D) and implementation planning (Phase F). The key distinction: Phase E says WHAT to do; Phase F says HOW to do it in detail.

Cross-Phase Concepts — Critical for the Exam

These concepts span multiple phases and are heavily tested. Understand them thoroughly.

Architecture Definition Document (ADD)

The ADD is the main architecture documentation artifact. It is NOT created all at once — it is built progressively:

Preliminary Phase → Framework documentation only (governance, tailoring)

Phase A → Statement of Architecture Work (the charter, not the ADD itself)
           Architecture Vision (separate document)

Phase B → Business Architecture sections added to ADD
           (Baseline Business Arch + Target Business Arch)

Phase C → Data Architecture sections added
           Application Architecture sections added
           (Both added during Phase C)

Phase D → Technology Architecture sections added
           (ADD now covers all 4 domains — complete for design purposes)

Phase E → ADD updated based on work package analysis
Phase F → ADD finalized
Phase G → ADD used as the compliance standard for implementation
Phase H → ADD updated with any changes

What the ADD contains:

  • Architecture Vision summary
  • Stakeholder Map and Concerns
  • Business Architecture (Baseline + Target)
  • Data Architecture (Baseline + Target)
  • Application Architecture (Baseline + Target)
  • Technology Architecture (Baseline + Target)
  • Architecture Views (each view created for its stakeholder viewpoint)
  • Rationale for key decisions
Exam tip

The ADD is built across Phases B, C, and D. It is NOT produced in Phase A. Phase A produces the Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work — these are separate documents, NOT the ADD.

Architecture Requirements Specification

The companion document to the ADD. While the ADD describes the architecture (qualitatively), the Architecture Requirements Specification quantifies it:

Architecture Definition Document (ADD) Architecture Requirements Specification
What Describes the architecture qualitatively Quantifies the requirements the architecture must meet
Content Views, models, descriptions Measurable requirements: performance, availability, security
Example "The application shall support multiple data sources" "The application shall process 10,000 transactions per second with 99.99% uptime"
Built in Phases B, C, D Phases B, C, D (in parallel with ADD)
Used in Phase G for compliance assessment Phase G for compliance assessment

Both documents are inputs to Phase G (Implementation Governance) where compliance is checked.

Gap Analysis — The Standard Technique

Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, and D. Understanding the technique precisely:

The Gap Analysis Matrix:

Needed in TO-BE? Not Needed in TO-BE?
Exists in AS-IS? RETAINED (keep unchanged) or CHANGED (modify/enhance) ELIMINATED (decommission/retire)
Does NOT Exist in AS-IS? ADDED (create new) N/A

Each cell of this matrix becomes a category of roadmap component:

ADDED      → "Build new Customer Portal application"
CHANGED    → "Enhance existing CRM with social media integration" (a.k.a. Improve)
RETAINED   → "Keep existing ERP system — no changes needed"
ELIMINATED → "Decommission legacy batch billing system" (a.k.a. Retire)
Exam tip

Gap Analysis produces four outcomes — Added, Changed, Eliminated, Retained (you may also see the synonyms Add / Improve / Retain / Retire). The Added, Changed, and Eliminated items become inputs to Phase E, where they are grouped into Work Packages (Retained items need no action). This same four-category vocabulary is used in Weeks 6–8 and on the exam.

Architecture Landscape

The Architecture Landscape is a key concept from the Architecture Repository (Part V). It classifies architectures at three levels:

Level What It Is Example
Strategic Architecture High-level, long-term capability roadmap "Our 5-year transformation plan"
Segment Architecture Detailed architecture for a specific business area "HR transformation architecture"
Capability Architecture Enabling architectural components shared across segments "Enterprise security architecture", "Enterprise data architecture"

Why this matters for the exam:

  • The ADM can be applied at any level (Strategic, Segment, or Capability)
  • When an exam question says "a business unit is doing its own architecture work" — that's a Segment Architecture
  • When a question says "the enterprise is doing a cloud security architecture" — that's a Capability Architecture

Multiple ADM cycles can run simultaneously at different levels of the Architecture Landscape.

Architecture Repository Structure

The Architecture Repository (part of Enterprise Continuum, Part V) stores all architecture artifacts. It has 6 layers:

Layer What It Stores
Architecture Metamodel The rules for how artifacts are structured and related
Architecture Capability Information about the Architecture Team: roles, skills, governance
Architecture Landscape The actual architectures: Strategic, Segment, Capability
Standards Information Base Industry standards, technology standards in use
Reference Library Reference architectures, patterns, best practices, guidelines
Governance Log Architecture decisions, waivers, compliance records
Exam tip

Know the 6 layers of the Architecture Repository, especially Governance Log (where waivers and compliance decisions are recorded) and Architecture Landscape (where the actual architectures live).

Week 2 Practice Quiz

25 Questions | Time: 40 minutes | Passing score: 20/25 (80%)

Questions are weighted to reflect exam emphasis: Phase A–E gets roughly equal coverage, plus cross-phase concepts.

Phase A Questions (Q1–5)

Q1. What formal document triggers the start of Phase A in the TOGAF ADM?

A) Architecture Vision
B) Statement of Architecture Work
C) Request for Architecture Work
D) Architecture Mandate

Answer: C — The Request for Architecture Work is the formal trigger for Phase A. It is issued by business/IT leadership. The Statement of Architecture Work is Phase A's OUTPUT (charter), not its trigger.

Q2. Which of the following BEST describes the Architecture Vision produced in Phase A?

A) A detailed technical specification of the target system
B) A high-level description of the target capabilities and business value to be delivered
C) A project plan for implementing the architecture
D) A compliance assessment against current standards

Answer: B — The Architecture Vision is deliberately high-level. It describes target capabilities and business value — enough to get sponsorship and approval. Detailed design happens in Phases B, C, D.

Q3. Phase A Step 11 requires the architect to secure approval before proceeding to Phase B. What document must be approved?

A) Architecture Vision
B) Communications Plan
C) Statement of Architecture Work
D) Architecture Definition Document

Answer: C — The Statement of Architecture Work is the formal project charter. It must be approved by the Architecture Sponsor before Phase B begins. This is a formal governance checkpoint.

Q4. TOGAF defines scope as having four dimensions. Which of the following is NOT one of the four dimensions of scope?

A) Breadth (which business units/functions)
B) Depth (level of detail required)
C) Stakeholder count (how many stakeholders are involved)
D) Time period (over what timeframe)

Answer: C — The four dimensions of scope are: Breadth, Depth, Time period, and Architecture Domains (which of the 4 domains are in scope). Stakeholder count is not a scope dimension.

Q5. What TOGAF technique is specifically recommended for developing the Architecture Vision in Phase A?

A) Gap Analysis
B) Value Chain Analysis
C) Business Scenarios
D) SWOT Analysis

Answer: C — Business Scenarios is the TOGAF-recommended technique for Phase A Architecture Vision development. It describes the problem, environment, actors, and desired outcomes. Gap Analysis is used in Phases B, C, D.

Phase B Questions (Q6–10)

Q6. Why must Business Architecture (Phase B) be completed before Data Architecture (Phase C)?

A) TOGAF regulations require this sequence without exception
B) Business Architecture defines what the organization does, which determines what data and applications are needed to support it
C) Technology Architecture must come after Business Architecture for legal reasons
D) Business Architecture requires Data Architecture as an input

Answer: B — Business drives everything. You cannot design the data architecture until you know what business processes the data must support. This is the foundational logic of the domain sequencing.

Q7. What is the difference between a Business Capability and a Business Process?

A) Business Capabilities are technical; Business Processes are non-technical
B) Business Capabilities describe WHAT the organization can do; Business Processes describe HOW it does it
C) Business Processes are documented in Phase B; Business Capabilities are documented in Phase C
D) They are equivalent terms used interchangeably in TOGAF

Answer: B — Capability = WHAT (stable, strategic). Process = HOW (operational, frequently changing). This distinction is important for Phase B design and gap analysis.

Q8. Which artifact does Phase B produce that shows all the things the organization is able to do, organized in a hierarchy?

A) Application Portfolio Map
B) Value Chain Diagram
C) Business Capability Map
D) Organization Chart

Answer: C — The Business Capability Map is a hierarchical diagram of all organizational capabilities. The Value Chain shows the sequence of activities creating value (Porter model). Organization Charts show reporting structure. Application Portfolio Maps are Phase C.

Q9. During Phase B Gap Analysis, an organization identifies that a customer service capability exists today but needs significant enhancement for the target state. How should this be categorized?

A) Added (new capability)
B) Eliminated (no longer needed)
C) Changed — exists but needs modification (also called Improve/Enhance)
D) Retained (keep as-is)

Answer: C — When a capability exists (AS-IS) AND is needed in the target (TO-BE) but must be modified, it is a Changed gap (also called "Improve/Enhance"). This becomes a candidate roadmap component. (The four gap outcomes are Added, Changed, Eliminated, Retained.)

Q10. At the end of Phase B, the architect adds Business Architecture documentation to a specific document that will grow through Phases B, C, and D. What is this document called?

A) Architecture Vision
B) Statement of Architecture Work
C) Architecture Requirements Specification
D) Architecture Definition Document

Answer: D — The Architecture Definition Document (ADD) is built progressively. Phase B adds the Business Architecture sections. Phase C adds Data and Application sections. Phase D adds Technology sections. By end of Phase D, the ADD covers all 4 domains.

Phase C Questions (Q11–15)

Q11. Within Phase C, what is the correct sequence of sub-phases?

A) Application Architecture, then Data Architecture
B) Data Architecture, then Application Architecture
C) The two are designed simultaneously
D) Data Architecture is designed in Phase B, not Phase C

Answer: B — Data Architecture is designed FIRST, then Application Architecture. You need to know what data exists before you can correctly design the applications that store and process it.

Q12. What does the Application Portfolio Map show?

A) The hierarchy of all organizational business capabilities
B) All applications in the organization, their business function, status, and relationships
C) The physical network topology connecting all applications
D) The sequence of steps in a business process

Answer: B — The Application Portfolio Map is the inventory of all applications: what they do, their lifecycle status (invest/tolerate/migrate/retire), and how they relate to each other and to business functions.

Q13. An organization discovers during Phase C that three different departments each maintain their own version of the "Customer" record in separate systems. The Data Architecture addresses this by identifying a single authoritative source for Customer data. What concept does this represent?

A) Data Flow Management
B) Master Data Management (MDM)
C) Data Virtualization
D) Application Integration

Answer: B — MDM addresses the problem of multiple, inconsistent copies of core business entities (Customer, Product, Employee, etc.) by establishing a single "golden record" as the master.

Q14. What is an Application Interface Catalog?

A) A list of all applications, their owners, and their business function
B) A catalog of all technical standards approved for use in applications
C) A list of all interfaces between applications, including protocol, direction, and data exchanged
D) A register of all vendors providing applications to the organization

Answer: C — The Interface Catalog documents how applications communicate: which systems talk to each other, what protocol they use (REST, SOAP, message queue, file transfer), in which direction, and what data is exchanged.

Q15. An organization's application landscape analysis reveals that two systems do exactly the same thing. One is newer, actively maintained, and used by the head office. The other is older, used by regional offices, and will soon lose vendor support. What action should be recommended for the older system?

A) Invest (enhance it to match the newer system)
B) Retain (keep as-is indefinitely)
C) Migrate (plan replacement by the newer system)
D) Parallel Running (run both systems indefinitely)

Answer: C — The older system should be marked for migration to the newer system. It has functional overlap, no future investment planned by the vendor, and a better replacement exists. Parallel Running is a temporary transition technique, not a permanent state.

Phase D Questions (Q16–19)

Q16. What TOGAF reference model is used in Phase D as the taxonomy for technology components?

A) III-RM (Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model)
B) Foundation Architecture (FA)
C) Technical Reference Model (TRM)
D) Enterprise Continuum

Answer: C — The Technical Reference Model (TRM) is TOGAF's reference model for technology architecture. It provides a standard taxonomy of technology services. The III-RM is also a TOGAF reference model but for information infrastructure, not the primary Phase D reference.

Q17. Which of the following is the CORRECT relationship between Application Architecture (Phase C) and Technology Architecture (Phase D)?

A) Technology Architecture is designed first; applications are then selected to fit the technology
B) They are independent; neither depends on the other
C) Application Architecture defines what applications exist; Technology Architecture defines the platform that runs them
D) Technology Architecture is only relevant for on-premise systems; cloud architecture is handled in Phase C

Answer: C — Applications run ON technology platforms. Phase C defines what applications exist and what they need; Phase D defines the technology infrastructure that runs those applications. The sequencing (C before D) reflects this dependency.

Q18. During Phase D, an organization is deciding whether to move from on-premise servers to a cloud platform. This is a decision about which component of the Technology Architecture?

A) Application Interface Catalog
B) Technology Standards and Platform Selection
C) Data Migration Strategy
D) Business Process Architecture

Answer: B — Cloud vs. on-premise is a platform/infrastructure decision, which is exactly what Technology Architecture (Phase D) addresses through technology standards and platform selection.

Q19. After completing Phase D, how many domains of the Architecture Definition Document (ADD) are complete?

A) 1 (only Business Architecture)
B) 2 (Business and Data)
C) 3 (Business, Data, and Application)
D) 4 (Business, Data, Application, and Technology)

Answer: D — Phase B adds Business Architecture, Phase C adds Data and Application Architecture, Phase D adds Technology Architecture. After Phase D, all 4 domains are documented in the ADD.

Phase E Questions (Q20–23)

Q20. Phase E is described as the "bridge" between architecture design and implementation planning. Which of the following BEST describes what makes Phase E distinct from Phases B, C, and D?

A) Phase E designs the architecture; Phases B, C, D implement it
B) Phases B, C, D design domain-specific architectures; Phase E consolidates gaps, creates work packages, and produces the first complete Architecture Roadmap
C) Phase E is the only phase that involves stakeholders
D) Phase E replaces Phase F when an organization is experienced with TOGAF

Answer: B — Phases B, C, D each design one domain and produce candidate roadmap components. Phase E integrates all of these into a coherent picture: consolidated gaps → work packages → transition architectures → Architecture Roadmap v0.1.

Q21. What is the version number of the Architecture Roadmap first produced as a complete, integrated document in Phase E?

A) Version 1.0 (final)
B) Version 0.1 (initial)
C) Version 0.5 (draft)
D) Version 2.0 (revised)

Answer: B — Phase E produces Architecture Roadmap Version 0.1. This is the first complete integrated roadmap but is still considered initial. It is finalized to the formal version in Phase F.

Q22. An organization is moving from a monolithic on-premise application to a cloud-native microservices architecture. The architect has defined two intermediate states: (1) the monolith migrated to cloud IaaS, (2) the monolith decomposed into services on cloud PaaS. What are these intermediate states called in TOGAF?

A) Work Packages
B) Phase Checkpoints
C) Transition Architectures
D) Segment Architectures

Answer: C — Transition Architectures are stable intermediate states between the current (AS-IS) architecture and the target (TO-BE) architecture. Each transition state is coherent enough to operate the business while more work continues.

Q23. A Work Package in Phase E is BEST described as:

A) A single deliverable for a software development project
B) A bundle of related implementation activities and deliverables that can be scheduled and assigned to a project
C) A document describing a single gap identified in Gap Analysis
D) A TOGAF governance artifact reviewed by the Architecture Board

Answer: B — A Work Package bundles related work together into an implementable unit. It has scope, deliverables, dependencies, estimated effort, and business value. It is more than a single deliverable and more than a raw gap.

Cross-Phase Questions (Q24–25)

Q24. Gap Analysis is performed in which phases of the ADM?

A) Only in Phase E, consolidating all domains at once
B) In Phases A, B, and C only
C) In Phases B, C, and D — once per domain
D) In all phases from A to H

Answer: C — Gap Analysis is formally performed in Phase B (Business domain), Phase C (Data and Application domains), and Phase D (Technology domain). Phase E consolidates the results of these three analyses. Phase A has readiness assessment but not a formal Gap Analysis of architecture domains.

Q25. The Architecture Definition Document (ADD) and the Architecture Requirements Specification serve complementary purposes. Which of the following BEST describes the difference?

A) The ADD is produced first; the Architecture Requirements Specification is produced after implementation
B) The ADD describes the architecture qualitatively (views, models, descriptions); the Architecture Requirements Specification quantifies measurable requirements (performance, availability, security)
C) The ADD is written by the architect; the Architecture Requirements Specification is written by the business
D) They are different names for the same document

Answer: B — The ADD describes WHAT the architecture looks like (qualitative). The Architecture Requirements Specification specifies HOW WELL it must perform (quantitative, measurable). Both are built progressively in Phases B, C, D and used together in Phase G for compliance checking.
